Tile z15 x9649 y12314 spans roughly 0.92 km of width at its latitude — computed from its metres-per-pixel (3.619 × 256 ≈ 926 m). The next tile east starts exactly where this one ends; the grid admits no gaps.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
The west/south/east/north geographic bounds of a z/x/y tile, by inverting the slippy-map formulas for its corner pixels.
Which map standard does it use?
The slippy-map standard (Web Mercator, 256-px tiles) shared by OSM, Google and MapLibre.
Can I use this in production GIS?
The formulas are the production standard itself — yes for web-mapping work.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 — tile systems are defined over it.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — tiles and pixels quantise; decimals beyond the cell are decoration.
Can I get bounds for a tile range?
Compute the corner tiles' outer edges — the range's extent is its northwest tile's west/north and its southeast tile's east/south.
TMS tiles?
Flip y first (y_tms = 2^z − 1 − y_xyz), then compute bounds — dialects differ, geography doesn't.
Bounds in projected metres?
The Web Mercator page converts the corners; tile edges are straight in Mercator space and very slightly curved in lon/lat space at large scales.
Polar tiles?
The grid caps at ±85.0511° — the top row of tiles carries that cap as its north edge.
Why does latitude span vary per row?
Mercator spacing: equal pixel rows cover shrinking degree spans as latitude rises — the bounds make the projection's rhythm visible.
